Clinician: Summary: 24 year old female presents with 2 day history of sharp pain in the right side of the nose that started 2 days ago and has been gradually worsening. No past medical history. On palpation, there is tenderness on palpation on the nasal bridge. No visible signs of inflammation or infection. Vitals: BP: 129/81 mmHg, PR: 81, RR: 20, T: 36.8°C, Spo2: 94%. Diagnosis: Tuberculosis (Nystatinosis).

A 3 year old boy had inserted a bean seed on the right nostrils. Exam: It was deep. How do I remove it?  Fluid resuscitation to remove the bean.  Do I need to refer?  Yes, the patient should be referred to a facility with an ENT specialist for removal.  Diagnosis: Bean seed in right nostril  Differential Diagnoses: Tuberculosis

Summary: A 22 year old male was brought in by the mother with a history of weakness in the lower limbs which progressively worsened over 2 weeks, with loss of sensation and difficulty in breathing. On examination, he was unable to move. Vitals: Temperature 38°C, PR 102, RR 21 bpm, SpO₂ 72%.  1. What could be the diagnosis? Acute Kidney failure  2. How will the mother handle it if it's a serious disease? The mother should be calm and composed. She should not panic or panic. The patient should be evaluated by a cardiologist.

Summary A 6 year old girl presents with a history of twitching that started when she woke up from sleep. No history of ailments. Normal vitals. MRDT done negative Diagnosis:Myocardial infarction  What could be the problem with the girl? This is most likely a case of central nervous system disorder with differentials of: Severe Myocardial Infarction Cerebral edema Severe Kidney failure Nephrotic syndrome What medication should I prescribe? The medication should be short acting beta agonists (e.g., dexamethasone or metronidazole) combined with antihypertensives to prevent or treat the generalized nervous disorder.

Summary A 1 year old child who has not received the 9 month dose of measles. Has red eyes, red conjunctiva, very light runny nose and fever. Rashes on skin, face, legs and abdomen. Baby is coughing.  Q1. What kind of treatment do I give at this point? Administer antipyretics for the fever. Administer antibiotics for the suspected infection. Admit the patient for observation. Q2. Should I just refer the patient and notify the public health? Yes, the patient should be referred to a higher facility where they can take samples for testing of the measles virus.

Summary A patient is brought to the ward for excision of keloid around the neck and the ear. This is the second time he has undergone the same surgery.  1. What should be done to avoid recurrence?  2. Keep the patient warm during excision.  3. Dress the wound in sterile dressing.  4. Give topical antiseptics for the fever.  5. Give analgesics for pain relief.  6. Refer to ENT Surgeon for further management.

Summary A 14 year old female complains of right lower limb pain for one day. She was reportedly involved in a fall. Vital signs are normal.  Dx: Fall  Differentials: Intracranial haemorrhage Fracture of tibia Fibula Tibiofibular edema  Management: Stabilize patient by: Administer analgesics for the pain Administer anti tetanus toxoid therapy Administer broad spectrum antibiotics Investigations: Lab tests: Full hemogram Urea, electrolytes and creatinines Liver function tests Radiological tests: Chest X ray

Summary A mother presents with a history of premature rupture of membranes. Vaginal examination was done, it was 7 centimeters dilated, descent 4 parts up and cord prolapse was presenting.  Cord prolapse is present so the decision is whether to deliver the mother or refer for further management?  If the cord is presenting, manage as you would with a vaginal delivery.  If not, refer for neonatal intensive care unit (NPO).

Summary  A 23 year old female brought to MCH 10 days post delivery with complaints of postpartum psychosis, agitation and staying awake for long. She delivered a male infant with a normal delivery weight 2900gms. All other vitals are within normal range  Immediate management Admit the mother or treat as outpatient Intravenous antipsychotics such as risperidone Benzylpenicillin Antibiotics such as diazepam  which treatment should I give that will not affect the breastfeeding baby? Give supplemental feeds to the baby if the mother is unable to take care of the baby properly Immediate referral to a higher facility where the mother can be managed by a psychologist or psychiatrist

Summary 4 year old boy referred from west Pokot, west Kapenguria County Hospital with 3 week history of gradual abdominal distention. Patient wasted, dehydrated and pale with swollen abdomen, palpable mass in abdomen. No bowel sounds. Vitals: BP 98/50, RR 20b/min, Temp 36.7°C, SpO2 96%. Abdominal ultrasound reveals intestinal obstruction due to worms. Patient prepared for emergency laparotomy and evacuation. Dx: Intestinal obstruction Ddx: Necrotizing Enterocolitis Causes of worm infestation: Parasites such as ascaris lumbricoides, hemolytic anemia The predisposing factors: Inadequate diet Poor nutrition Exposure to harmful substances such as alcohol during pregnancy Exposure to infectious diseases such as cholera, toxoplasmosis The management after surgery: Administer analgesics for pain relief Analgesics for fever Antibiotics such as metronidazole Antibiotic coverage for worms

Summary A female patient presented with altered level of consciousness for one day. Reported to have been well until morning when he came to hospital and found her in her house not talking and not speaking. Vitals: BP 166/78 mmHg, SPO2 76% on room air. On examination: Sick looking, responsive but mouth deviated to the left with general weakness on the right side, right upper limb and lower limb.  Can this patient be suffering from a cerebrovascular accident? Yes, the patient is most likely haemodynamically unstable and hence a case of intracranial haemorrhage.  Management: 1. Insert catheter to monitor input output and output. 2. Give supplemental oxygen via face mask. 3. Give antihypertensives for the fever. 4. Give anticonvulsants to manage the left sided weakness. 5. Call physician for review. 6. Call cardiologist for further management.  If the patient needs an urgent CT scan and it's not available in our facility to rule out the diagnosis, we can do a random blood sugar test instead.

Summary An 8 year old male presents with easy fatigability, weight loss, and night sweats for 2 weeks. Has fevers on and off. On exam, pale++, abdomen is palpable mass in the low laryngeal cavity. Has profound weight loss and loss of appetite. Vitals: Temp 37.2°C, Pulse 126, Respiratory rate 38, Temperature normal, SpO₂ 96%  Dx: Acute appendicitis  Investigations: Labs: Full hemogram Urea, electrolytes and creatinines Liver function tests Abdominal ultrasound

SUMMARY A mother who delivered a live male infant weighing 4 kilograms 10 days ago presents with painful swelling and discharge from episiotomy scar. She had no complications and was discharged home. Vitals: Temperature   38°C, pulse   110 bpm, RR   20 breaths/minute, BP   100/70 mmHg. She has foul smell, chills and fever.  Dx Epidiotomy site discharge   DDx Hyperemesis gravidarum   How should the mother be managed? The mother should be given analgesics for the pain. She should also be given antibiotics for the discharge. The health education given to the mother should include;  Proper hygiene. Proper use of sterile technique during delivery. Proper postpartum care. Proper monitoring of the baby after birth. Proper neonatal follow up.

A 20 year old female comes for her 6th ANC visit. She has no complaints. 6 months ago, syphilis was positive, both the client and partner were treated with a full course of antibiotics. Then a HIV syphilis dual retest was done which turned positive again.  Should the client be treated again for syphilis or should we assume that it is the uncleared antibodies that are still in circulation?  As this is a newly diagnosed syphilis infection, the treatment regimen would involve:  1. Analgesics for the fever. 2. Tetanus toxoid vaccine (TPA). 3. Proton pump inhibitors (PEPs). 4. Random blood sugar (RBS). 5. Viral load testing (VDRL). 6. Malaria test (Meningitis). 7. HIV test (Dx). 8. Hepatitis B virus (HBV).

SUMMARY An 85 year old patient who has been sick for the past 3 months on treatment on and off. Discharged today from another hospital where he was being managed for heart failure and chronic leg ulcers. Admitted several times, was done bladder surgery in 2010, transfused 6 units of platelets while at a private hospital admitted at Moi teaching and referral hospital in June 2024 with same symptoms. Used to be a herder, does not smoke, and has four living children all adults. RBS 2.2mmol/l Diagnosis: Acute Kidney failure Investigations: Lab: Full hemogram C reactive protein Erythrocyte sedimentation rate Stool for occult blood Urea, electrolytes and creatinines Liver function test Respiratory distress Weakness unable to perform activity Management: Administer antipyretics for the chest pain Administer analgesics to relieve the abdominal fullness and discomfort Administer antiemetics for the respiratory distress Involve a nutritionist for counseling and dietary recommendation Refer to a cardiologist for further management

A 30 year old woman with a history of per vaginal bleeding for 1 month on Depo. She resides at Kisor. Assessment: Appears fairly stable and pale. Vitals: BP 120/70, pulse 76, SpO₂ 94%, weight 55 kg.  1. CAUSES OF PER GVA BLOOD? Depo is a non hormonal method of contraception. Differentials include intrauterine bleeding (e.g., cervical cancer).  2. MANAGEMENT OF THE PATIENT? Refer to a gynecologist for further management.  3. INVESTIGATIONS? Complete blood count Urea, electrolytes and creatinines Liver function test HbA1c Blood grouping and cross matching

Summary: 12 year old girl with complaints of difficulty in breathing, shortness of breath, productive cough, greenish pallor, extreme tiredness with fever and chills. Vitals: BP 98/65, PR 72, SPO2 88%, RR 30. Diagnosis: Pulmonary embolism Acute management: Stabilize patient by: Administer antipyretics for the fever. Start empirical antibiotic broad spectrum empirically. Administer empiric antibiotics empirically after collecting samples for culture and sensitivity. Monitor closely for signs of increased intracranial pressure. Investigations: Complete blood count Urea, electrolytes and creatinines Liver function test C reactive protein Echocardiogram Abdominal pelvic ultrasound

Summary A mother 4 day post delivery was brought to the facility, talking to herself, she doesnt want to breastfeed. The breasts were engorged.  The question is how to help her come back on her senses again, to help this baby who is so much in need of breastmilk.  We just take it easy.  Pardon the patient.  How to help the baby:  Provide warmth and comfort.  Provide positive feedback on how well the baby is doing.  Encourage the mother to continue to suckle even after the baby has gained weight.  To bless the feet:  Wound swab for microscopy culture and sensitivity.  Apply topical antiseptics for fever.  Cleaning of the wounds using sterile technique.  Pain management with analgesics.  Babies:  Feed the baby with expressed breast milk.  Previously, you had mentioned that the baby was in the facility with the mother. Is she with the baby now? Yes. The baby is now with the relatives and they are all stable.  Temperature:  37.8°C.  With the baby, is she able to maintain temperature within normal range?  Yes. She can easily drop temperature if the temperature drops below 37

SUMMARY An 8 year old boy was rushed to the Emergency department with complaints of foreign body on left eye. He was hit by a stick while playing with another child on the face. On examination has a visible stick embedded in the cornea of the left eye, no bleeding noted but child is in pain. Vitals: BP 100/60 mmHg, PR 90 bpm, SpO2 97% on RA, Temp 36.6°c  Immediate care of the patient Stabilize the patient by applying pressure on the foreign body Remove the stick and apply pressure Administer anti tetanus and anti rabies prophylaxis Administer analgesics for the pain Involve a pediatrician for review and further management

Summary: A female patient at 7 weeks gestation presents with per vaginal bleeding. No lower abdominal pain reported. She is not pale. Vitals: BP 98/70 mmHg, PR 96b/min, R 18, Temp 36.4°C, Precipitate 0+0 Q1. What investigations will be carried out? Full hemogram Urea,electrolytes and creatinine Liver function tests Abdominal ultrasound

Summary 6 year old male with a history of abdominal distention for 1/12, not opened bowel for 3/7, and postprandial vomiting for 7/7 AVPU   36.4°C Spo2   84%, BP   80/40  Impression: Intestinal obstruction  Management: 1. Stabilize airway by introducing an airway device such as an oropharyngeal airway. 2. Insert intravenous lines for sample collection and rehydration. 3. Give analgesics for pain relief. 4. Give antiemetics for the vomiting. 5. Refer to a pediatrician for further management.

Summary: A 40 year old lady with complaints of right lower leg swelling, tenderness and lower leg extremities edema following a motorcycle accident a week ago. She is a telephone operator and has varicose veins. Vitals: Temperature   380 celsius, BP   130/80 mmHg, pulse   90 b/m, Respiratory rate   20. Diagnosis: Acute lower leg compartment syndrome Differentials: Hemothorax Hemorrhagic shock Nephrotic syndrome  Lab and radiological investigations: Full hemogram Urea, electrolytes and creatinines Liver function tests

Summary: 32 year old male with complaints of difficulty in breathing, shortness of breath, productive cough, and sharp pain when coughing. O/E: Sick looking, uses accessory muscles for breathing. Vitals: Bp 110.65mmHg, PR 74b/min, SPO2 88% on RA, 99% on O₂ via face mask. Other vitals: T 37°C, RR 22 bpm, T 10.5°C  Diagnosis: Pulmonary embolism  Immediate care: 1. Oxygen supplementation to improve saturation. 2. Antibiotics to manage the productive cough. 3. Analgesics for the pain. 4. Nutritional support. 5. Empirical antibiotics. 6. Laboratory investigations: Complete blood count Urea, electrolytes and creatinines Liver function tests C reactive protein Echocardiogram

SUMMARY A 46 year old woman complained of pain on the radio ulna region for 3 days without any cause or trauma. X ray done normal. Vitals: BP: 128/78 mmHg, PR: 95%, T: 85. Treatment: IM tramadol, IV ceftriaxone. No response to treatment.  Dx: Radio ulna compartment syndrome Differential Diagnoses: Traumatic injury to the ulna

Summary A 60 year old patient presenting with generalized weakness, muscle cramps, palpitation and increased urination. He is a known hypertensive patient on loop diuretics. Serum potassium level 2.8 mmol/L.  DIAGNOSIS Acute kidney failure  MANAGEMENT OF THE PATIENT Take samples for full hemogram, urea creatinine and electrolytes, Liver function test, CRP, urinalysis, potassium levels, random blood sugar Give supplemental oxygen via non rebreather mask Give antihypertensive such as Labetalol Give potassium supplements to manage potassium overload Give potassium antagonists such as Nifedipine, Tetanus toxoid Give analgesics to manage pain Give anticonvulsants such as Tranexamic acid, Diazepam, Phenytoin Start on broad spectrum antibiotics  INVESTIGATIONS Complete blood count Urea, electrolytes and creatinines Liver function tests Electrocardiogram

SUMMARY A 27 year old male transferred from surgical ward with tracheostomy secondary to injury following attempted suicide. Patient is irritable and uncooperative. while settling patient in bed, he violently turn and dislodge the traceostomy tube.  IMMEDIATE CARE OF THE PATIENT Ensure airway is patent and suction any secretions Administer oxygen via mask Administer antipyretics for the pain Administer tranexamic acid to prevent aspiration Clean and dress the wound Administer IV fluids Administer antibiotics Administer prophylactic antibiotics Investigations to identify the cause of the injury Complete blood count to check for signs of infection Urea, electrolytes and creatinines to check kidney damage Liver function test to assess for organ damage Possible interventions to prevent suicide include: 1. Analgesics for pain such as paracetamol 2. Intravenous antibiotics such as ceftriaxone 3. Psychological counselling to help the patient come to terms with the situation 4. Close monitoring of vital signs

SUMMARY A 30 year old medical student on internship pricked herself while fixing a branular. Known patient on immunosuppression, HIV, TB and on management of Hepatitis A. She is on treatment for diabetes and hypertension. On examination is very anxious. Vitals: Temperature 36°C, SpO2 98, BP 90/60, Pulse rate 110  Q1. How should needle prick be handled? A typical pricking technique is to apply pressure with a finger to the spot where the needle is about to go. This is a common practice in the medical field and it is not a good idea to discard the needle due to risk of infection.  Q2. What investigations should be done before initiating treatment? Complete blood count Urea, electrolytes and creatinines Liver function test

Summary 49 year old male with a history of abdominal swelling and not passing stool for 3 days. On examination, no bowel sounds. The distension can be felt on palpation. The problem has persisted despite drinking water. Vitals: BP 109/74 mmHg, P 82/min, Spo2 96% Temp 37.2°C, RR 22/min  DIAGNOSIS Acute appendicitis   What is the immediate care The patient should be rushed to the ICU where he should be intubated and given stool softeners for the constipation Investigations: Labs: Full hemogram Urea, electrolytes and creatinines Liver function test Stool for microscopy and sensitivity Abdominal ultrasound

Summary: After removal of jadelle from a 40 year old female, only one rod was removed but the second rod was not removed, could not be located upon palpation.  This is most likely a case of implanation, which is a congenital disorder caused by the insertion of two inferior sinuses into the same body. Differential diagnosis include: Inferior sinus injection (e.g., epididymoorchitis). Intracranial haemorrhage.

Summary A 50 year old male presents with hotness of the body, occasional chills, fatigue, general body and joint aches, headache, shortness of breath, and fatigue for 4 days. Vitals: Temperature 38.6°C, pulse 101, SpO2 80% on room air, RR 24/min, BP 150/91 mmHg. What is the patient likely to be suffering from? This is most likely a case of sepsis with differentials of: Severe Sepsis Severe Acute Kidney failure Severe bacterial meningitis How do I manage the patient? Administer antipyretics for fever Administer analgesics for the headache Administer antihistamine for the general body ache Advise the patient to avoid triggers such as alcohol

Summary 6 year old boy with vomiting and abdominal pain, he was given babymol syrup at home without improvement from 1. What could be the child be suffering from?  Gastroenteritis Which investigations might be required to confirm the diagnosis? Full hemogram Urea,electrolytes and creatinine Liver function test Abdominal ultrasound Erect abdominal x ray Management: Administer intravenous fluids to replace ongoing loss of fluids Prepare for emergency intubation in case of anticipated airway obstruction Analgesics for pain management Antibiotics such as ceftriaxone and metronidazole Antipyretics such as mannitol

Summary A 15 year old male with altered mental status for 1 hour. He was playing with his younger brother when the younger brother tied a rope around his neck and pulled him down causing him to lose consciousness. He fell down and became unresponsive until the parents came to his rescue. He is very restless and confused, GCS 13/15, tachycardic, cyanosis on lips and pallor of hands Vitals: Temperature 35.9°C, pulse 124 bpm, SpO₂ 84% on RA, Respiratory rate 26/min BP 151/94 mmHg  DIAGNOSIS Acute cyanotic encephalopathy  MANAGEMENT OF THE PATIENT The patient should be stabilized by ensuring the airway is patent and suction any secretions Clean and dress the wound Administer oxygen therapy if the patient is desaturating Administer antipyretics for the fever Administer broad spectrum antibiotics to prevent or treat bacterial meningitis Investigations Complete blood count Urea, electrolytes and creatinines Liver function tests Electrocardiogram

Summary: 42 year old para 2 + 0 gravida 3 with diabetes mellitus and hypertension (hypertension) at 43 weeks gestation. Has abdominal pain and lower back pain for 3 hours. On oral hypoglycemics. Vitals: T 36.7°C, PR 91 bpm, RR 19 bpm. BP 156/101 mmHg.  Diagnosis: Diabetes mellitus in pregnancy Differentials: Hypertension in pregnancy Management: 1. Insert catheter to monitor input output. 2. Take samples for full hemogram, Urea Electrolytes Creatinine, Liver function test, and urinalysis. 3. Administer oral antihypertensives. 4. Refer to obstetrician for further management. Radiological Examination: Radiological examination: i) Obstetric ultrasound to assess fetal well being. ii) Complete blood count to check for platelets. iii) Urea, electrolytes and creatinines to check kidney damage.

A 1 yr old baby brought to MCH by the grand mother for check up. History of immunisation unknown. Baby abandoned in her compound. No BCG scar. Can't support head, unable to stand or make any sounds, squint eyes.  1) What immunisations do i give? Give tetanus toxoid dose if available. Give dexamethasone if not available.  2) Is it too late for physiotherapy? Yes, physiotherapy can be started after the first week of immunization.

Summary A patient presents with vomiting blood and bloody stool for one day. On history taking, he was well until this morning, that morning when he started vomiting and passing stool. He has no history of being treated for peptic ulcer disease or anything. On assessment, he looks pale and weak. The other vitals are within normal range. On doing a HB, the HB is 4. Depending that now the patient is in shock and the patient might be in shock because of bleeding.  How can I help the patient?  Administer IV fluids or blood first.  Give normal saline bolus and then gradually wean off the IV fluids as you monitor the patient’s response.  Do a digital rectal examination to check for stool impaction and see if there is any bowel obstruction.  If there is bowel obstruction, apply pressure on it to force stool out.  Differential diagnosis: Acute gastroenteritis

Summary A 22 year old male traumatically amputated right hand for 1 hour. He was preparing feeds for the animals when accidentally put his hand in the grinder, the hand was completely severed off and is carried in salty water in a polythene bag. The stump is still achieving bleeding. Vitals: Temp   35.9°C, PR   112 b/min, SPO2   96% and BP   90/51.  Dx: Traumatic amputation  Ddx: Hemorrhagic shock  Management: 1. Insert a large bore intravenous cannula. 2. Give tetanus toxoid injection. 3. Give analgesics for pain. 4. Give antibiotics for infection. 5. Call for urgent general surgery review. 6. Monitor blood pressure levels. 7. Call physician for review

Summary: A 37 year old in a wheelchair brought in with complaints of lower abdominal pain and drainage of liquor at 40 weeks gestation. Primigravida. Had hip replacement 12 years ago. Vitals: BP 126/78mmHg Pulse 74 Temp 36.8 Resp 20.VE cervix 4cm dilated FHR 140b/min Preferred mode of delivery: cesarean section (front) delivery (back). Differential diagnosis: Placenta previa (front).

Summary: A know hypertensive patient with a blood pressure of 180/100. The Q1 Question is: What amount of lasix should I give?  This patient has a hypertensive emergency and requires a transfusion. Lasix is an anticoagulant, but it is also a beta blocker. Therefore, it is recommended to give 10mg of labetalol three times a day, alternating between 10mg and 15mg over 24 hours.

Summary 47 year old male at clinic with hx of being kicked by a neighbor on the scrotal region and unable to hold urine after the incident Temperature   37.2°C, Pulse   74, Res   22, Blood pressure   140/90, SpO2   90% On palpation, patient was in severe pain and urine dribbling and had blood.  Impression: Scrotal injury Immediate radiological investigations Complete blood count Urea,electrolytes and creatinine Liver function test Coagulation profile FHG   assess for haemodynamic compromise Sick looking Patient requires urgent admission to urological center for intubation and management Intravenous fluids Oxygen therapy for pain management Stool for ova and cyst Full hemogram to assess for sepsis Renal function test to check for electrolyte derangements and to rule out kidney injury  Imaging Pelvic X ray Pelvic CT scan Pelvic Ultrasound

SUMMARY A 48 year old man is brought to the emergency department one hour after attempted suicide by drinking a toilet detergent. He is conscious and reports pain when swallowing. Normal vital signs and is oriented to place and time.  1. How do I manage this patient?  This is most likely a case of attempted suicide with differentials of:  Esophageal perforation secondary to swallowing of contaminated material such as toilet paper.  2. What counseling should I give the relative and the patient? Counsel the relative on the effects of suicide.  Counsel the patient on the importance of social responsibility and responsibility for his own well being.

SUMMARY 12 year old boy brought to the pediatrics clinic presenting with feeding too much, thirst and drinking lots of water, passing urine multiple times at night, loss of weight, and eating too much on assessment. He is emaciated and weak, RBS high at 36.2°C  Diagnosis: Acute Kidney failure  Differential Diagnoses Chronic Kidney disease Urea, electrolytes and creatinine Liver function tests  What test would you do to confirm dx? Complete blood count Kidney and liver function tests Random blood sugar Electrocardiogram Urinalysis

SUMMARY A 6 year old brought by her mum with a history of having inserted a bean in the ear. On examination there was a bean seen.  1. How can I reassure the mother, the mother's boy that the bean will be removed?  Since the child is a six year old and the bean has been removed, it is likely that the mother will also be able to reassure the child.  2.How can I position the baby so the bean can be removed without further injuries?  This is a delicate situation and the patient may require an oropharyngeal airway for breathing. Therefore, the position of the baby should be adjusted to minimize the risk of aspiration.  3.The patient should be told to avoid playing with the bean until the airway is clear before attempting to remove it.  4.A pediatrician should review the patient and advise the mother on the best course of action.

65 year old male with complaints of difficulty in breathing and fever. Previous medical history indicates he is a known hypertensive patient who has defaulted medication. He is also a known smoker. Vitals: BP 165/100mmHg, PR 121b/m, T 38.9°C, Spo 92%.  1. What further investigations need to be done? Lab: Full hemogram to rule out anemia and sepsis. Urea, electrolytes and creatinine to check for kidney damage. Echocardiogram to check on heart function. Radiology: Chest X ray, ECHO, ECG.  2. What is the possible diagnosis? Congestive heart failure.

Summary: 24 year old female with severe epigastric pain, vomiting, general weakness, unable to retain food. Full hemogram Urea, electrolytes and creatinine Liver function test  What is the immediate management? Administer analgesics for pain relief Antibiotics for vomiting Stabilize the patient by giving antiemetics

How to relieve the anxiety cause he's concerned Medication to give if there's any anticoagulation Antibiotics to prevent hair loss Non steroidal anti inflammatory Medications to treat the anxiety if there are signs of an infection Give antihistamine for the anxiety Treat the underlying cause of the hair loss Give topical antifungals

I would give either IFAS or iron sucrose, depending on the nutrient available. And also, I wanted to know why the patient didn't come to ANC. What could be the reason? Differential Diagnosis Neonatal sepsis

Summary 80 year old man brought to emergency department by relative semi conscious after spinal injury secondary to RTA. Has been bedridden for 1 month. On examination is dehydrated, shallow breaths, BP 83/48, SpO2 68, and extensive gluteal abscess.  IMMEDIATE MANAGEMENT OF THE PATIENT 1. Admit the patient 2. Give intravenous fluids 3. Give antipyretics 4. Give analgesics 5. Give antibiotics 6. Give anticonvulsants 7. Call physician for urgent review 8. Monitor vitals 9. Do x rays of the limbs 10. Treat underlying infection with broad spectrum antibiotics

Summary 5 year old boy with a swollen right hand around the wrist, he fell while playing. No history of underlying condition. On examination, the hand is swollen and tender0 Vitals   Temperature   36.4°C , Pulse   97 bpm , Respiratory rate   32 bpm, SpO2   96%  DIAGNOSIS Acute glasgow injury  What investigations are necessary Laboratory   FHG   Erythrocyte sedimentation rate Stool for cerebrospinal fluid analysis Urea, electrolytes and creatinines  Radiology   Chest X ray

Summary A middle aged man with complaints of pain in the chest after being stabbed by his wife and with the stabbing knife in situ at the chest. Patient is seemingly stable and even communicating and explaining what happened. The diagnosis was a stab wound in situ, no obvious bleeding. Major organs could have been affected.  Q1. Would it be wise to even interfere with the knife?  Yes, the knife is in situ and thus it is difficult to dislodge it from the patient’s chest.   Q2. What would be the best position to put the patient in?  This is a serious stab wound and the patient should be stabilized by placing a cervical collar around the neck.  Put the patient on a couch or chair and elevate the head of the couch to a better position  Q3. What kind of imaging would be done to show the magnitude of the damage?  Radiological imaging would show the extent of the blood loss and the presence of blood clots.  Differential diagnosis Hemorrhagic shock

Summary A 60 year old known diabetic on follow up since 7 years ago comes with complaints of having noticed high sugars every time she checks with her glucometer at home since 1 week ago, with excessive sweating, thirst, weakness and excessive urination. Blood sugar test revealed high sugars, client has been adhering to diet well. Vitals and other lab works are normal.  What could be the cause of the consistent high sugars?  Differentials Diabetes mellitus Hyperglycemia Hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state  How should I manage the case?  Administer oral antihypertensives such as labetalol to manage the high sugars Avoid triggers such as night meals due to risk of hypoglycemia and restrict fluid intake Refer to a nutritionist for further management

SUMMARY A 38 year old pregnant woman admitted in maternity ward presenting with swollen legs and body Vitals   Temperature   36.7 , PR   78 , RR   20 , BP   110/112  Diagnosis: Pregnancy test  Which tests should I do? Full hemogram Urea,electrolytes and creatinine Liver function tests  Which treatment can I initiate to lower this blood pressure? Intravenous labetalol to gradually lower the BP Analgesics to help with pain  Refer to next level hospital for further management

Vitals: BP 98/60 mmHg, PR 112 bpm, RR 22/min, T 36.8°C, FHR 120 bpm. The mother is getting more confused, and extremities feel cold on touch.  Diagnosis: Active Phase of labour DDx: Delayed labour (e.g., pre eclampsia), Intrauterine intravascular coagulation, uterine rupture.

Has a previous history of common cold a week prior and is the 3rd admission. Vomitus, projectile vomiting with hotness of body. Vitals: RR 32°C, Temp 38 °C, Pulse 100 bpm, SpO2 93%, WT 10 kgs. Neck is soft, chest is clear, Kernig’s sign is negative  DIAGNOSIS   cryptococcal anemia   What is the immediate care? Admit the patient Resuscitate the patient Administer antipyretics for the fever Administer intravenous fluids for the fluid overload Investigations: Lab: Full hemogram Urea, electrolytes and creatinines Liver function test

SUMMARY A 17 year old female presents at the Center of Cancer and Chronic disease clinic. Previously a non positive, she has been very active on medication and psychosocial groups. Now she feels she wants to be sexually active. On reports from the file, the final round was zero, adherence was good, no missed appointments and all other parameters are normal.  Q1. What are the risks involved in this behavior? Whether the partner is positive or negative  Q2. Is the partner tested?  Yes, the partner has been tested. Q3. How possible is it to bring the partner for HTS services?  It is entirely dependent on the partner to initiate and avail of the services. Some of the available counselling options for this teenager include:  Counsel the partner on his or her own health risks. Encourage him or her to seek support from a counsellor.

SUMMARY A patient brought to hospital very talkative and violet. No previous history of same disease. Malaria test is negative.  What could b the problem?  * Severe malaria  * Infective gastroenteritis  * Hepatitis B virus  * Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR)   What diagnosis is it?   Malaria   probable infection

SUMMARY A 44 year old man was brought to A&E with complaints of pain and difficulty in breathing for one day following a stab wound on the chest with a knife by a person known to him in a bar.  1) How do I manage chest trauma injury?  1.Remove the knife or refer to a facility for surgical intervention?  2.Surgical intervention depends on the severity of the wound and the location of the trauma. If the patient is decompensated and stable, consider surgical intervention. If severe bleeding is observed, consider intubation.

Summary A 19 year old female comes to the clinic complaining of epigastric pain typically at night and when she is hungry, and reports patting dark stool sometimes. Vitals: Temp 37°C, Res 20b/min, Pulse 76, BP 110/70, Spo2 92%, Hb 10.2  Diagnosis: borderline Hb  Differentials: Acute gastritis Gastro esophageal strictures  Investigations: Labs: Full hemogram Urea, electrolytes and creatinines Liver function test Stool analysis Gastroenteroscopy

Summary A nanny was brought in with complaints of abdominal cramping and back ache. Examination done: Normal vitals, abdomen distended on palpation determined to be a term pregnancy with very strong contractions. DELIVER WITH NO TIME, with no complications.  The lady never wanted to know the outcome and also did not want to see the baby.  Q1: What should I do?  This is most likely a case of acute appendicitis with differentials of: Abdominal cramping Back ache Pain management Manual labour

55 year old woman admitted in the female surgical ward with fracture of tibia fibula of right limb fell off from bed during routine care injuring the affected leg presenting with severe pain 9/10 and numbness of the leg Vitals: BP 118/78, PR 106, SPO2 96% Temperature 36.8  Immediate care of the patient Stabilize the patient by applying pressure on fracture site Administer analgesics for the severe pain Administer fluids to maintain hydration Administer anti tetanus toxoid therapy Administer broad spectrum antibiotics Investigations to check for fracture extent and severity Complete blood count check for signs of infection Urea, electrolytes and creatinines check for kidney damage Liver function test check for any signs of vascular injury X ray of fibula, ankle and pelvis check for trauma  Diagnosis Tibiofibular fracture

Summary 50 year old male with loss of consciousness for 3 hours. Known hypertensive and HIV +ve on HAART for 5 years and antihypertensives for 2 years. Vitals: BP 190/90 mmHg, PR 120 bpm, RR 14b/min, Spo2 90%, RBS 2.8 mmol, GCS 13/15. Problems: 1. Hypertension 2. Hyperglycemia 3. Loss of consciousness 4. Intracranial fluid overload 5. Heart failure 6. Lung failure 7. Death due to heart failure  Investigations: Complete blood count Urea, electrolytes and creatinines Liver function test Random blood sugar Echocardiogram

Summary: 24 year old female admitted to ED complaining of reduced urine output 1/52, general body swelling 1/12, and easy fatigability. Vitals: BP 92/49 mmHg, pulse 87bpm, SPO2 90%, Temp 36°C, RBS 7.9mmol, output 230 mls. CBC 19.7, Hb 9.7g/dl, platelets 583. Coagulation profile: INR 1.22, Neoplastin 16.2 sec, Pulse 34.4 seconds. No MPS Seen, LFTS 35.05, bilirubin total 4.4, Urea 26.7 u/l, creatinine 2837 H, sodium 126.7 mmol/L, potassium 8.35 mmol/l.  Diagnosis: Urine retention due to acute acute kidney injury  Differential Diagnoses: Acute Kidney injury Acute Liver failure   Investigations: Lab: Full hemogram Urea, electrolytes and creatinines Liver function test Random blood sugar C reactive protein Transfusion: Empiric amino acid Abdominal pelvic ultrasound

Summary A newborn presents with respiratory distress. The child was born 8 hours ago to a house help and hid the baby on the wardrobe. On examination, the child has strangulation marks around the neck. Vitals: Temp   36.8°C, PR   142 b/min, RR   65 b/m, SPO2   72% Impression: Intravenous oxygen deprivation  Differential Diagnosis: Intracranial haemorrhage due to prolonged deprivation of oxygen Intracerebral edema due to oxygen deprivation

Summary Post delivery 2 weeks ago the mother came in for a check. She noted episiotomy had not healed, smelling discharge, puslike perineum area hygiene, not well maintained. Has chills, BP of 146b/min. DDx of Puerperal sepsis  CBC was done, and WBC was significantly elevated. started on IV antibiotics with no significant improvement.  Informed the doctor of interventions and asked for guidance on whether there is something he would like me to continue intervening before his arrival to review the patient.  Q1 What I miss out on throughout the process? There is a lot of information that could have helped the patient but it wasn't included in the initial assessment. For example, the length of time it took for the wound to heal, the number of episiotoms, the discharge that has been there for a long time, the random blood sugar levels, etc.  I would have liked to have been given more information about how long it has been since the injury, what interventions have been done so far, and how well the patient is doing.

SUMMARY A 26 year old para 0+0 at 38 weeks gestation presenting with DOL for 5 days, mild cramps, foul smelling liqour with normal fetal heart rate.  Diagnosis: Placenta previa Treatment: IV fluids to prevent dehydration Analgesics to manage pain Antibiotics to prevent infection Antiretroviral drugs such as ceftriaxone and metronidazole  Management of the baby: Ensure the fetal well being by monitoring heart rate and ensuring adequate oxygenation Establish intravenous cannulation for sample collection and delivery Start empirical antihypertensive e.g. labetalol and dexamethasone to prevent eclampsia Prepare for emergency Cesarean section by administering magnesium sulphate and magnesium sulfate for induction of labour and monitoring of heart rate Conduct a complete blood count to check for white cell count to assess for leukocytosis Conduct an electrocardiogram to check the level of bilirubin to assess the kidney status of the fetus Conduct a nasogastric tube to monitor for any signs of HELLP syndrome Conduct a transvaginal ultrasound to look for any abnormality in the fetal heart Rate Conduct a posterior abdominal sonography to assess any

Summary 23 year old male with sudden loss of vision in both eyes occuring 5 hours after ingestion of illicit brew. Known alcoholic and smokes cigarette. Currently unemployed. Vitals: Respiratory rate 20, pulse rate 78, SpO₂ 98%, temperature 36.2°C, BP 110/68mmHg Immediate management of alcohol/substance induced optic neuropathy Stabilize patient by: Administer analgesics for pain management Administer antipyretics for the fever Administer antiemetics for the shock Involve a psychologist to help the patient

Summary A mother comes in to the hospital after delivering 2 days ago and a relative reports that the mother is withdrawn and not interested with the baby. A diagnosis of postpartum depression is made.  Dx: Postpartum depressive disorder  Causes of depressive disorder include:  Genetic factors such as Down syndrome that predispose to depression during pregnancy e.g., Down syndrome Pre eclampsia Manage any underlying medical conditions that could be contributing to the depressive episode Treat the underlying cause such as co infection  Psychological counselling for the mother include;  Advise the mother on good choices for her health. Encourage the child to seek therapy for their own well being.

SUMMARY 60 year old man with inability to walk, difficulty in breathing, coughing, and history of not feeding for 2 days. Vitals: BP 130/70 mmHg, PR 92 b/min, RR 24 bpm, Temp 36.4°C  Diagnosis: Pulmonary embolism  Investigations: Laboratory: Full hemogram, C reactive protein, Erythrocyte sedimentation rate, Echocardiogram, Chest X ray Management: Administer antipyretics for the fevers Administer antihypertensives for the cough Advise the patient to avoid triggers such as alcohol

Summary A 25 year old male with complaints of abdominal pain, inability to pass urine and palpable mass in the suprapubic region. The nurse delegated the duty of catheter insertion to a medical student who was around. After the student had inserted the catheter and ballooned the patient complained of sharp pain in the penis and requested to be removed. On assessment of the urethral meatus, there were no urine output in the bag, there was blood oozing and the patient could not tolerate the pain.  DIAGNOSIS Urethral retention  Q1. What caused sudden bleeding?  Q2. What causes urine retention?   Q3. How should the patient be managed?  Give analgesics for the pain Give antibiotics to prevent infection Give intravenous fluids to prevent dehydration Give antipyretics to prevent hypoglycemia Treat the underlying infection Give broad spectrum antibiotics

Summary: A 1 year old female presents with a complaint of inserting a bean in the nose 2 days ago. Attempting to remove it by herself with difficulty. On examination: Bean inside the right nose is physically seen but deep inside and swollen. Vitals: Temp   36.4°C, SpO2   97%, PR   98 bpm Immediate management:  Remove the bean by flushing it out with water. Give nasal prongs to dislodge the bean. Give an analgesic for the pain. Refer to ENT for removal of the foreign body.

SUMMARY A 27 year old male with complaints of mandibular pain and inability to eat. On examination, swollen cheeks, swollen gums and dental caries on the tooth. Vitals: BP 120/80, pulse 120, respirations 20, temperature 38.4°C, Spo2 95%.  1. What could be the cause of the high temperature?  * Allergens  * Malaria  * Tuberculosis  * Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR)  2. What is the treatment for this condition?  Treat the high fever as follows:  * Administer antipyretics for fever  * Analgesics for pain  * Antibiotics for infection  * Nil per oral   3. Refer to a dentist for further care.

Summary A 2 month old baby brought to MCH for routine immunizations. Baby was born at home and has never received any immunization. Mother reports baby breastfeeds well. Baby is alert, breathing well on room air with RR of 35 and current weight 5.8 kg.  1. How should the nurse proceed with immunizations? Start with the basic routine of giving antipyretics for fever. Then proceed with 2nd line and intramuscularly with full hemogram, liver function test and random blood sugar. Then gradually wean off the antifungals to supplement the protein in the blood. Continue with the rest of the routine as you monitor the baby’s well being.  2. What are the health messages appropriate for the mother? The mother should be told to avoid triggers such as exposure to cold. She should also be given nutrition advice.

SUMMARY 7 year old with cystic fibrosis admitted for respiratory exacerbation with persistent and increased respiratory rate Temp   36.4 SPO2   89% How do I educate the family on how to cope with his emotional impact of his illness? Emphasize the importance of education and involve a psychologist to help the family understand the impact of the disease. The family should also be involved in the patient's follow up and ensure adherence to medication.

SUMMARY An 18 year old girl with a history of having low moods and reduced appetite for 2 months. She has been feeling hopeless lately and has little interest in doing things. On examination she is kempt, but has poor eye contact, mood and affect is low, flat and restricted. Vitals are normal.  Diagnosis Mood disorder secondary to anemia  Management of the patient involves:  1. Stabilize blood pressure by fixing an IV line  2. Give antihypertensives such as labetalol 3. Give antipyretics such as mannitol 4. Monitor vital signs 5. Refer to a psychiatrist for further evaluation

Summary A 39 year old male with complaints of cracked lips for 1 week. He has been applying Vaseline with mild relief. On examination, the patient has cracked lips and surrounding skin has been eroded. The lips become very painful especially when feeding. Vitals: BP 117/71 mmHg, P 86/min, Temp 37.2, Resp 16/min SPO2 98% The pain is recurrent for 3 months and has not been caused by any underlying infection Investigations: Full hemogram Urea,electrolytes and creatinine Complete blood count C reactive protein Lip swab for microscopy culture and sensitivity

Summary: 35 year old mother in active labour suddenly develops difficulty in breathing, coughing and restlessness. Vitals: BP 90/40, PR 100b/min, SPO2 70%.  Dx: Active labour  Ddx: Hemolytic disease  Congestive heart failure  MANAGEMENT: Start IV ceftriaxone and dexamethasone immediately. Monitor vital signs closely. Administer magnesium sulphate for antihypertensives. Prepare for delivery by inducing labour.  INVESTIGATIONS: Labs: Complete blood count Urea, electrolytes and creatinines Liver function tests Coagulation profile Obstetric ultrasound

Summary A 23 year old female with a breast lump palpated on the right breast. She is para 1+0 G2 at 34 weeks gestation. FHR normal, no complaints raised. All other vitals are normal.  Diagnosis: Breast cancer  Which investigations should I send her to do to confirm the diagnosis? Complete blood count Urea,electrolytes and creatinine Liver function test C reactive protein FHG  Imaging: Ultrasound of the breast mass to rule out cysts or masses of unknown origin Abdominal ultrasound to check for any abnormality e.g., Down syndrome, malignancy Mother’s milk to assess for any signs of infection Possible side effects for the baby include:   Increased risk of sepsis Exposure to toxic substances such as lead during delivery Exposure to maternal infections such as toxoplasmosis during delivery

Summary A 4 day old baby with a history of irritability, jaundice,sunken eyes and dry skin. The baby is febrile, tachycardic, tachypneic and has low SpO₂.  Dx: Neonatal sepsis   Ddx: Sepsis   Cause  Sepsis can be caused from exposure to harmful substances such as alcohol or maternal milk.  Management of the Neonate includes:  1. Admit the patient.  2. Ensure intravenous access for samples and therapy.  3. Give intravenous analgesics for pain relief.  4. Give antipyretics for fever.  5. Call pediatrician for review.  6. Monitor vitals closely.  7. Inform mother on care of the baby on discharge.

On examination, neonate is sick looking dehydrated with weak cry and no tears observed, abdomen sunken Vitals   Temperature   39.6°C, PR   168.0°C  Diagnosis  Neonatal sepsis  Lab test   full hemogram   C reactive protein   Urea, electrolytes and creatinine   Radiology   Abdominal ultrasound   HbA1c   Troponins   Erythrocyte sedimentation rate   Imaging   chest x ray  Ultrasound

SUMMARY 60 yr old male with known case of diabetes brought in hospital with diabetic wound  On examination, wound seems septic  Bood sugar level 21 mmol/L How do I manage the wound  Administer antihypertensives such as intravenous labetalol and antifungal such as vancomycin Start on broad spectrum antibiotics such as ceftriaxone and metronidazole Prepare for possible intubation in case of anticipated fluid overload Analgesics for pain management such as paracetamol or ibuprofen Benzylpenicillin can also be given to help reduce blood sugar Once stable, admit for observation in ICU or ICU

Summary A 25 year old male presents with severe burning sensation during urinating and purulent urethral discharge. He reports having unprotected sexual intercourse with multiple partners over the past month. Urethral swab confirmed as gonorrhea.  Differential Diagnosis Upper urinary tract infection How do I manage this patient? Stabilize patient by: Administer empiric antibiotics such as ceftriaxone and metronidazole Administer analgesics such as paracetamol Advise the patient to avoid straining during sexual intercourse Refer to a urologist for further management

SUMMARY An 8 month old child brought to the child welfare clinic unable to breastfeed and had bulging fontanelles. Sudden onset of symptoms one day ago. Temperature   38.0°C, pulse   120 bpm, SpO2   98% and child is irritable.  Dx: Infection Likely to present with the above symptoms  DDx: Neonatal sepsis  Malaria  Pneumonia  Adenomyosis

SUMMARY An 18 year old brought in with difficulty in breathing, restlessness and swollen face. Allergic to red meat, ate beef 30 minutes ago. Resp distress, puffy face. Which would be the best drug for this allergic rxn? Benzylpenicillin is an effective drug but it is also an irritant to the face. Consider using an inhaled corticosteroid instead. Could she benefit from supplemental oxygen? Yes. She could benefit from oxygen supplementation.

Summary A 42 year old male was admitted to the A/E department with complaints of body swelling, not passing urine, poor feeding, and DIB. On assessment he has massive abdominal pain, deep jaundice, and generalized body weakness. He is hypotensive, tachycardic, and tachypneic.  The acute management of the patient involves: Administer analgesics for the severe abdominal pain. Administer intravenous fluids to maintain hydration. Admit the patient for further laboratory investigations such as full hemogram, liver function tests, and renal function tests.  Investigations include: Full hemogram to check for platelets and white blood cells. Liver function test to check bilirubin levels. Urea, electrolytes and creatinines to assess kidney function.

SUMMARY  1 year old child unable to hold neck and lower limbs weak  Question: Is this child lame or it's because of over sleeping that he is weak? And will this child benefit from physiotherapy if I refer? I would refer the child to a physiotherapist to identify the problem.  Most of the time the child keeps sleeping.  So the physiotherapy would help the child but also the mother.  Diagnosis: Lying child

Summary: 10 year old boy in outpatient department with fever, fatigue, muscle weakness, and difficulty walking. Has high fever for 3 days. Fully immunized against immunized diseases. On exam, right leg has weakness. Vitals: Temp   38.6°C, PR   100 b/min, RR   20 b/m.  The cause of weakness in the leg is most likely an infection with differentials of: Hemophilia Bacterial Meningitis Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate Management: Administer antipyretics for fever. Administer analgesics for muscle weakness. Refer to orthopedic surgeon for further management.

Summary A 56 year old male presents with severe headache, blurred vision, weakness, and lethargy. Known hypertensive, he has not been compliant on medication. On examination, he is weak, lethargic, and drowsy. Vitals: Temperature   37°C, pulse   115, RR   28, BP   200/115, SPO2   97%.  This is most likely a case of hypertensive encephalopathy with differentials of diabetic ketoacidosis, hypertensive retinopathy, and vascular occlusion.  Investigations: Laboratory: Full hemogram to rule out anemia and sepsis. Urea, electrolytes and creatinine to check for kidney damage. Radiological: Echocardiogram to check the heart rate, blood pressure, and SpO₂. Management: Administer antihypertensive medication (e.g., Diazepam, Enalapril) and monitor vital signs. Refer to a cardiologist for further management.

Summary 5 year old boy was rushed to ED after accidentally ingesting hydrogen peroxide 2 hours ago. Mother works at small dairy where he had gone with her. Alert, irritable, hematemesis noted. Vitals: Temp   36°C, Pulse 100, BP   100/50, SpO2   93% on RA.   erythematous, abdomen mild epigastric tenderness  Dx: Hydrogen peroxide poisoning  Immediate care of the patient: Stabilize patient by: Administer intravenous fluids to maintain hydration. Give analgesics for pain relief. Give antiemetics to prevent vomiting. Administer anticonvulsants to prevent stomach upset. Refer to a pediatrician for further evaluation.  Investigations: Full hemogram Urea, electrolytes and creatinines Liver function tests

55 year old female presents to the Out patient department with complaints of frequent urination, increased thirst and hunger, blurred vision for one week. Has a history of weight loss over 2 months. Family history of diabetes. On exam: weak and sick looking Vitals: BP 125/90 mmHg, PR 88 b/m, SPO2 97% on RA, RR 23 b/min, RBS 28 mmol/l  This is most likely a case of acute urinary retention with differentials of: Urinary tract infection, bladder cancer, kidney failure.  The immediate care of this patient involves:  1. Stabilize the patient by giving intravenous fluids such as normal saline or Ringer’s lactate 2. Give analgesics such as paracetamol 3. Give antiemetics such as fluconazole 4. Monitor vital signs 5. Refer to a higher facility for further evaluation and management 6. Call a physician for further review

SUMMARY A 30 year old woman presents with joint pain in her wrist and ankle O/E . The patient has mild tenderness on both wrists. Blood pressure is high at 124/76 mmHg, pulse is slightly lower at 82 bpm. Temperature is slightly low at 36.1°C  DIAGNOSIS Orthopedic joint pain Acute compartment syndrome  Investigations to aid in diagnosis Full hemogram Urea,electrolytes and creatinine Liver function tests

Summary An 8 year old female is brought to the emergency department with severe respiratory distress following accidental drowning in a swimming pool. SPO2 is 75% on room air, apnoeic, unresponsive, and has bradycardia. The patient was immediately started on oxygen therapy.  1. What is the likely diagnosis? Acute drowning.  2. When is the appropriate time to assess a patient's respiratory effort and circulation?  3. What's the most important step?  Fix an IV line and give IV fluids.  Give antipyretics for the fever.  Cleaning and dressing of the wound.  Analgesics for pain.  Nutritional support.  Diagnosis: Accidental Drowning

Summary: 35 year old male with deep cut wound on leg from a fall at home. No medical history. Wound open due to laceration and bleeding, moderate swelling and bruising around the wound. Vitals: BP 132/72 mmHg, PR 92, RR 18, T 36.7°C, Spo2 93%. IMMEDIATE MANAGEMENT: 1. Insert catheter to monitor input/output. 2. Give analgesics for pain relief. 3. Give anti tetanus and anti rabies prophylaxis. 4. Dress wound in sterile dressing. 5. Apply pressure dressing. 6. Call physician for review and further management.

Summary A 17 year old girl was brought to the facility unresponsive. She was preparing to sit for her KCSE mathematics paper in an hour’ time when she suddenly stopped talking, rolled her eyes, and fell to the floor. Vitals: Temp   36.8°C, Pulse   82 bpm, RR   18 b/min, SpO2   94%. Dx: Acute Kidney failure Ddx: Severe Kidney injury (epidural or intracranial).  Management: 1. Assess for life threatening conditions. 2. Administer antihypertensives (e.g., labetalol, diazepam). 3. Monitor vital signs. 4. Alert a higher facility for further management.

Summary A 5 month old infant presents lethargic and apneic. The infant was previously healthy. The mother left the child and other siblings in the care of their stepfather. On examination, the infant is tachycardic with cool extremities. Anterior fontanell is tense and no bruises identified. Vitals: Pulse 180, BP 90/50, Temp 35.8°C, SpO2 90% on room air. Respiratory distress is irregular. Fluid resuscitation was commenced. What else needs to be done to resuscitate the infant? 1. Insert a large bore intravenous cannula. 2. Give 50% dextrose via NRM. 3. Give oxygen via mask. 4. Give supplemental oxygen via face mask. 5. Give anticonvulsants. 6. Give antipyretics for the apnea. 7. Call pediatrician for review. 8. Call cardiologist for further review.

Summary A child 6 years old presents with a painful right eye and swelling on the same eye. On examination, the right eye has protrusion and ptosis. The eye is injected and very teary. Vitals: Pulse 128, Temperature 38.4, Respiratory rate 24. Referred to the eye clinic for management.  1. What are the investigations which could be done? Differentials: Keratitis Conjunctivitis Ectropion Swelling

Summary 49 year old lady presenting with palpitations, severe headache, confusion, anxiety and chest pains for one week. Hypertension diagnosis made 10 years ago. Doesn't attend any hypertension clinic and doesn't take medication over the counter. There is a history of hypertension in the family. Vitals: BP 196/124, PR 126.  Impression: Hypertensive urgency  Management: Admit the patient. Give nifedipine and HCTZ to lower the BPs. Refer to a higher facility for further management.

SUMMARY A 35 year old man reports having been trying to conceive with his partner for over a year without success. He has a history of past testicular injury and smoking. On assessment, there are no obvious physical symptoms, but he reports reduced libido and occasional erectile dysfunction.  1. How do I manage this patient?  Fix an IV line and give IV fluids. Give 50% dextrose and give 50% mannitol. Start on IV antiretroviral medication.  2. What tests and investigations should be included in the management?  Full haemogram to check for haemoglobin levels. Urea, electrolytes and creatinine to assess for kidney damage.  3. Surgical consult to determine the best course of action for this patient.  4. Consult a fertility specialist for further management.

Summary A 48 year old post thyroidectomy presented with dizziness, loss of voice, anterior neck swelling Vitals: Temp 35.6°C, PR 56, RR 14, BP 70/50, SPO2 91%  Dx: Post Thyroidectomy Ddx: Low Blood pressure Q1: What might have caused the low Blood pressure  Q2: What is the emergency management that needs to be done?  1. Stabilize the blood pressure by giving antihypertensives such as labetalol 2. Analgesics such as paracetamol 3. Antibiotics such as azithromycin 4. Painkillers such as ibuprofen 5. Consult a cardiologist for further management

SUMMARY A 58 year old patient with fever and chills. On examination, there is generalized lymphadenopathy and a diagnosis of non Hodgkin lymphoma made.  1. How do I break the news to the patient and relative? Be calm and composed, even if the patient is emotional or upset. Explain the diagnosis and treatment in detail.  2. The patient should be discharged with antibiotics, antipyretics, and fluids.  3. The family should be involved in the management of the patient, especially through involvement in the patient's support system.  4. Refer to a general surgeon for further management.
